title: AC Bridges
short_intro: AC bridges are network circuits used to measure unknown impedances, inductances, capacitances, and frequency using null detection methods with alternating current sources. They operate on the principle of balancing complex potential drops across bridge arms.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Basic conditions for bridge balance, application to simple Maxwell and de Sauty bridges, and frequency-independent balance equations.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Complex impedance balancing, derivation of bridge balance conditions for Maxwell's inductance-capacitance bridge, Schering bridge, Wien bridge, and Wagner ground connection.

prerequisites: Series and parallel L-C-R circuits in alternating current
Conditions for bridge balance in Wheatstone network

concept_notes.heading: Principle of AC Bridge Balance
bullets: An AC bridge consists of four arms containing complex impedances Z<sub>1</sub>, Z<sub>2<sup></sup></sub>, Z<sub>3</sub>, and Z<sub>4</sub>, an AC source, and a null detector (such as headphones or an electronic voltmeter).
At balance, no current flows through the detector, meaning the potential difference across the detector terminals is zero.
The fundamental balance equation is given by the product of opposite arm impedances being equal: Z<sub>1</sub>Z<sub>4</sub> = Z<sub>2<sup></sup></sub>Z<sub>3</sub>.

concept_notes.heading: Complex Balance Condition
bullets: Since impedances are complex quantities expressed as Z = R + jX, the bridge balance equation Z<sub>1</sub>Z<sub>4</sub> = Z<sub>2</sub>Z<sub>3</sub> must hold in both magnitude and phase.
Equating real parts and imaginary parts yields two independent balance conditions that must be satisfied simultaneously.
This implies that balancing an AC bridge generally requires two variable components (such as a variable resistor and a variable capacitor or inductor).

concept_notes.heading: Maxwell's Inductance-Capacitance Bridge
bullets: Used for measuring an unknown inductance in terms of a known standard capacitance.

One arm contains an unknown inductor with resistance r<sub>1</sub> and inductance L<sub>1</sub> in series with a resistor R<sub>1</sub>, while the opposite arm contains a standard capacitor C<sub>3</sub> in parallel with a resistor R<sub>3</sub>.
Yields independent balance equations for both resistance and inductance, meaning the balance is independent of supply frequency.

concept_notes.heading: Schering Bridge
bullets: Primarily used for the measurement of unknown capacitance, relative permittivity (dielectric constant), and dissipation factor (dielectric loss) of capacitors.
Features a standard mica capacitor in one arm and a parallel combination of a variable resistor and variable capacitor in the adjacent arm.
Extremely precise for high-voltage applications because the loss angle can be directly determined from the resistance and capacitance values at balance.

concept_notes.heading: Wien Bridge
bullets: Used for measuring audio frequencies and as a frequency-determining network in oscillators.
Contains series and parallel RC combinations in adjacent arms.
The balance conditions depend explicitly on the angular frequency ω of the AC supply.

derivations.title: General Balance Condition for an AC Bridge
derivations.conditions: Four arms with complex impedances Z<sub>1</sub>, Z<sub>2</sub>, Z<sub>3</sub>, and Z<sub>4</sub> forming a closed loop with an AC detector between opposite junctions.
steps: Let an alternating voltage E be applied across diagonally opposite corners of the bridge network.
At balance, the current through the detector connected across the other two diagonal corners is zero.

Therefore, the current flowing through Z<sub>1</sub> must equal the current flowing through Z<sub>3</sub> (let it be I<sub>A</sub>), and the current through Z<sub>2</sub> must equal that through Z<sub>4</sub> (let it be I<sub>B</sub>).
Equating the potential drops across the two arms meeting at a detector terminal: I<sub>A</sub>Z<sub>1</sub> = I<sub>B</sub>Z<sub>2</sub>.
Using the other pair of arms: I<sub>A</sub>Z<sub>3</sub> = I<sub>B</sub>Z<sub>4</sub>.
Dividing the two equations eliminates the currents: (Z<sub>1</sub> / Z<sub>3</sub>) = (Z<sub>2</sub> / Z<sub>4</sub>).

derivations.title: Maxwell's Inductance Bridge Derivation
derivations.conditions: Arm 1: L<sub>1</sub> and r<sub>1</sub> in series with R<sub>1</sub>; Arm 2: Pure resistance R<sub>2</sub>; Arm 3: Pure resistance R<sub>3</sub>; Arm 4: Parallel combination of R<sub>4</sub> and C<sub>4</sub>.
steps: Write complex impedances for each arm: Z<sub>1</sub> = (R<sub>1</sub> + r<sub>1</sub>) + j&omega;L<sub>1</sub>, Z<sub>2</sub> = R<sub>2</sub>, Z<sub>3</sub> = R<sub>3</sub>, and 1/Z<sub>4</sub> = (1/R<sub>4</sub>) + j&omega;C<sub>4</sub>.
Substitute into the balance condition Z<sub>1</sub>Z<sub>4</sub> = Z<sub>2</sub>Z<sub>3</sub>, which can be rearranged as Z<sub>1</sub> = Z<sub>2</sub>Z<sub>3</sub>(1/Z<sub>4</sub>).
Substitute the explicit terms: (R<sub>1</sub> + r<sub>1</sub> + j&omega;L<sub>1</sub>) = R<sub>2</sub>R<sub>3</sub> [ (1/R<sub>4</sub>) + j&omega;C<sub>4</sub> ].
Equate real parts: R<sub>1</sub> + r<sub>1</sub> = R<sub>2</sub>R<sub>3</sub> / R<sub>4</sub>.
Equate imaginary parts: &omega;L<sub>1</sub> = R<sub>2</sub>R<sub>3</sub>&omega;C<sub>4</sub>, leading to L<sub>1</sub> = R<sub>2</sub>R<sub>3</sub>C<sub>4</sub>.
derivations.result: L_1 = R_2 R_3 C_4 	ext{ and } r_1 =  rac{R_2 R_3}{R_4} - R_1

formula_sheet.name: General AC Bridge Balance Equation
formula_sheet.variables: Z<sub>1</sub>, Z<sub>2</sub>, Z<sub>3</sub>, Z<sub>4</sub> are complex impedances of the four bridge arms.

formula_sheet.name: Maxwell Bridge Inductance
formula_sheet.variables: L = unknown inductance, R<sub>2</sub>, R<sub>3</sub> = resistance arms, C = standard capacitance.

formula_sheet.name: De Sauty Bridge Capacitance
formula_sheet.variables: C<sub>1</sub> = unknown capacitance, C<sub>2</sub> = standard capacitor, R<sub>1</sub>, R<sub>2</sub> = non-inductive resistors.

formula_sheet.name: Schering Bridge Unknown Capacitance
formula_sheet.variables: C<sub>1</sub> = test capacitor with loss, C<sub>3</sub> = standard capacitor, R<sub>2</sub>, R<sub>4</sub> = bridge arm resistances.

formula_sheet.name: Schering Bridge Dissipation Factor
formula_sheet.variables: D = dissipation factor (tan &delta;), &omega; = angular frequency, C<sub>4</sub>, R<sub>4</sub> = parallel components.

formula_sheet.name: Wien Bridge Frequency
formula_sheet.equation_html: f =  rac{1}{2pi sqrt{R_3 R_4 C_3 C_4}}
formula_sheet.variables: f = frequency of AC source, R, C = arm resistance and capacitance values.
formula_sheet.conditions: Bridge arms symmetrical such that R<sub>3</sub> = R<sub>4</sub> and C<sub>3</sub> = C<sub>4</sub>.

formula_sheet.name: Complex Impedance Expression
formula_sheet.equation_html: Z = R + jleft(omega L -  rac{1}{omega C}ight)
formula_sheet.variables: R = resistance, L = inductance, C = capacitance, &omega; = angular frequency, j = imaginary unit.

formula_sheet.name: Detector Sensitivity Condition
formula_sheet.variables: S = sensitivity, &#916;I = detector current change, &#916;Z = impedance imbalance.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Wagner Earthing Device Circuit Setup
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A bridge network with an additional auxiliary RC branch connected from the detector junction to ground.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Eliminates errors due to stray earth capacitances between bridge components and ground by ensuring the detector terminals are at ground potential at balance.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested conceptually in PGT exams regarding precision bridge measurement errors.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Null Detector Response Curve
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A plot of detector current or deflection versus variable resistance/capacitance setting showing a sharp minimum at the balance point.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows how sharpness of null depends on bridge component tuning and detector sensitivity.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used to explain experimental precision in finding balance.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Wien Bridge Frequency Response
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A plot of output-to-input voltage ratio against frequency f, peaking sharply at the resonance frequency f<sub>0</sub>.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates frequency selectivity used in audio oscillators.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently asked in PGT application-based questions.

solved_numericals.question: In a de Sauty bridge used to compare two capacitances, the arm resistances at balance are R<sub>1</sub> = 400 Ω and R<sub>2</sub> = 800 Ω. If the standard capacitor C<sub>2</sub> has a value of 0.5 μF, find the unknown capacitance C<sub>1</sub>.
solution_steps: Recall the balance condition for de Sauty bridge: C<sub>1</sub>R<sub>1</sub> = C<sub>2</sub>R<sub>2</sub>.
Rearrange the formula to solve for C<sub>1</sub>: C<sub>1</sub> = C<sub>2</sub> (R<sub>2</sub> / R<sub>1</sub>).

solved_numericals.question: A Maxwell's inductance bridge is balanced with the following component values: R<sub>2</sub> = 1000 Ω, R<sub>3</sub> = 1000 Ω, R<sub>4</sub> = 500 Ω, and C<sub>4</sub> = 0.2 μF. Calculate the unknown inductance L<sub>1</sub> and its effective series resistance r<sub>1</sub> assuming R<sub>1</sub> = 0.
solution_steps: Use the Maxwell bridge balance formula for inductance: L<sub>1</sub> = R<sub>2</sub>R<sub>3</sub>C<sub>4</sub>.
Substitute the values: L<sub>1</sub> = 1000 × 1000 × 0.2 × 10<sup>-6</sup> H = 0.2 H.
Use the resistance balance formula: r<sub>1</sub> = (R<sub>2</sub>R<sub>3</sub> / R<sub>4</sub>) - R<sub>1</sub>.
Substitute the values with R<sub>1</sub> = 0: r<sub>1</sub> = (1000 × 1000) / 500 = 2000 Ω.

solved_numericals.question: In a Wien bridge oscillator network, the frequency-determining arms consist of equal resistors R = 10 kΩ and equal capacitors C = 10 nF. Determine the frequency of oscillation.
solution_steps: The frequency formula for a symmetrical Wien bridge is f = 1 / (2&pi;RC).

assumptions_and_limitations: AC sources are assumed to be purely sinusoidal with negligible harmonic distortion; presence of harmonics prevents a true sharp null.
Stray capacitances and mutual inductances between bridge leads can introduce measurement errors unless shielded and grounded properly (Wagner earth).
Components are assumed to be linear; nonlinear elements cause bridge balance to depend on signal amplitude.

common_misconceptions.wrong: An AC bridge can be balanced by adjusting a single variable resistor.
common_misconceptions.correct: Balancing an AC bridge generally requires independent adjustment of two variables to satisfy both magnitude and phase (real and imaginary) conditions.
common_misconceptions.why: Complex impedance matching requires simultaneous real and imaginary part cancellation.

common_misconceptions.wrong: All AC bridge balance conditions depend on the frequency of the AC source.
common_misconceptions.correct: Certain bridges like Maxwell's inductance-capacitance bridge have balance equations independent of frequency.
common_misconceptions.why: When the frequency term cancels out algebraically in both real and imaginary balance equations, frequency does not affect the balance point.

quick_revision: General AC bridge balance condition is Z<sub>1</sub>Z<sub>4</sub> = Z<sub>2</sub>Z<sub>3</sub>.
Maxwell bridge measures unknown inductance using a standard capacitor: L = R<sub>2</sub>R<sub>3</sub>C.
Schering bridge measures high capacitance and dielectric loss factor.
Wien bridge is used for audio frequency measurement and oscillator frequency determination.
Wagner earthing device eliminates stray earth capacitance errors in sensitive bridge circuits.
